text: The name we say every day comes from that low ground.
Chicago is a French spelling of a Miami-Illinois word, shikaakwa, for the wild leek that grew thick in the river bottoms.
In 1687 one of La Salle's men wrote that the place was called Chicagou because of the quantity of wild garlic in the woods.
The city is named for an onion.
The United States arrived as a garrison.
In 1803, soldiers under Captain John Whistler built Fort Dearborn at the mouth of the river.
A sandbar shaped like an elephant's trunk blocked the harbor, so the river bent south and ran parallel to the lake before it found a way out.
The garrison did not hold the ground easily.
In 1812 the fort was evacuated and destroyed in a battle with Potawatomi warriors, then rebuilt four years later.
For most of three decades that fort was nearly all that passed for a town.
The land changed hands on paper first.
In 1816, at Portage des Sioux on the Mississippi, the same Three Fires nations signed the Treaty of St.
Louis and ceded a strip about twenty miles wide running from the lake to the Illinois River, the exact ground a canal would need.
They drew it as the Indian Boundary Line.
A few Chicago streets still run on that old diagonal, off the grid, because they trace a line that predates the grid.
